claims.text: High-entropy nanoalloys have superior high-temperature structural stability compared with lower-entropy alloys.
High-entropy nanoalloys have superior high-temperature chemical stability compared with lower-entropy alloys.
Mixing multiple principal elements creates lattice distortions.
The lattice distortions arise from atomic-size mismatches among the mixed elements.
Lattice distortions increase the activation energy for atomic diffusion.
An increased diffusion activation energy limits atomic mobility at high temperature.
Reduced atomic mobility suppresses phase segregation.
Reduced atomic mobility suppresses grain coarsening.
Reduced atomic mobility limits chemical degradation during high-temperature exposure.
After identical annealing, the high-entropy nanoalloy will have a lower atomic diffusion rate than the binary or low-entropy baseline.
After identical annealing, the high-entropy nanoalloy will exhibit less grain growth than the binary or low-entropy baseline.
After identical annealing, the high-entropy nanoalloy will retain a more homogeneous phase and elemental distribution than the binary or low-entropy baseline.
A binary or low-entropy nanoalloy has lower configurational entropy than an equiatomic multi-principal-element nanoalloy.
A binary or low-entropy nanoalloy has less pronounced lattice distortion than the proposed high-entropy nanoalloy.
The prediction is expected to apply to nanoscale alloys annealed at approximately 700–900 °C in an inert atmosphere.
At temperatures outside the proposed range or under reactive conditions, alternative stabilization mechanisms may operate.
The magnitude of diffusion retardation depends on the particular atomic-size mismatches and elemental combinations.
Diffusion coefficients can be compared using in-situ TEM or tracer techniques.
Grain growth and phase or elemental uniformity can be compared using electron microscopy, XRD, and EDS mapping.
